questions.question: I wrote an event subscriber class in my plugin but Shopware never calls it. How do I register it correctly?
Which bin/console commands install and activate a plugin I just created?
questions.answer: Refresh the plugin list first with `bin/console plugin:refresh` [1]. Then install and activate the plugin with `bin/console plugin:install --activate SwagBasicExample` [1]. Replace `SwagBasicExample` with your plugin's name [1][2]. Clear the cache afterwards with `bin/console cache:clear` if needed [4].

questions.question: How can I scaffold a new plugin from the CLI, and which files are always generated?
questions.answer:
Run the plugin generator from your Shopware project root, passing the plugin name:

```bash
bin/console plugin:create SwagBasicExample
```

[3]

The command asks for a plugin name and namespace (both UpperCamelCase) if you do not pass them as arguments, then asks whether to scaffold optional files [3]. To skip optional scaffold files, pass the namespace and `--no-scaffold`:

```bash
bin/console plugin:create SwagBasicExample 'Swag\BasicExample' --no-scaffold
```

[1]

The plugin is created in `custom/plugins`; use `--static` to create it in `custom/static-plugins` instead [3].

The files always generated are `composer.json`, the plugin base class, `config.xml`, `.gitignore`, and the PHPUnit setup [3]. These are the files an extension needs to be installable [3].

questions.question: Where does the config.xml for a plugin settings page go and what is the minimum it has to contain?
questions.answer:
Create the file at `src/Resources/config/config.xml` inside your plugin. [2] The minimum it must contain is at least one `<card>` element with a `<title>` and at least one `<input-field>` [1], and each `<input-field>` must contain at least a `<name>` element [1]. Minimal example:

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<config xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
        xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/shopware/shopware/trunk/src/Core/System/SystemConfig/Schema/config.xsd">
    <card>
        <title>Minimal configuration</title>
        <input-field>
            <name>example</name>
        </input-field>
    </card>
</config>
```
[1]

questions.question: How do I read a value from my plugin's configuration inside a PHP service?
questions.answer:
Inject `Shopware\Core\System\SystemConfig\SystemConfigService` into your service through the DI container, then call `get` with the prefixed key `<BundleName>.config.<configName>`. [1] For example, inject it in `services.php` with `service(SystemConfigService::class)` and add a constructor parameter: [1]

```php
$services->set(MySubscriber::class)
    ->args([service(SystemConfigService::class)])
    ->tag('kernel.event_subscriber');
```
[1]

```php
$exampleConfig = $this->systemConfigService->get('SwagBasicExample.config.example', $salesChannelId);
```
[1]

Set `salesChannelId` to `null` to apply the configuration to all Sales Channels, or pass a specific Sales Channel ID. [1] Using the bare key `example` is discouraged because multiple plugins could define a field with the same technical name. [1]

questions.question: What classes and service tags do I need to create a scheduled task in a plugin?
questions.answer:
You need a task class that extends `Shopware\Core\Framework\MessageQueue\ScheduledTask\ScheduledTask` and implements `getTaskName` and `getDefaultInterval` [1], plus a handler class that extends `Shopware\Core\Framework\MessageQueue\ScheduledTask\ScheduledTaskHandler`, is annotated with `#[AsMessageHandler(handles: ExampleTask::class)]`, and implements `run()` [1]. Both are registered in `<plugin root>/src/Resources/config/services.php`, which must sit in a `Resources/config/` directory relative to the plugin's base class [2]. The task is registered with the tag `shopware.scheduled.task` and the handler with the tag `messenger.message_handler` [2].

Example wiring:

```php
$services->set(ExampleTask::class)
    ->tag('shopware.scheduled.task');

$services->set(ExampleTaskHandler::class)
    ->args([
        service('scheduled_task.repository'),
        service('logger'),
    ])
    ->tag('messenger.message_handler');
```
[2]

questions.question: How do I create a database migration for my plugin and which method should contain the schema changes?
questions.answer: Generate the migration skeleton from your Shopware root directory with `./bin/console database:create-migration -p SwagBasicExample --name ExampleDescription` [3]. This creates a class in `<plugin root>/src/Migration/` that extends `MigrationStep` and contains `getCreationTimestamp()` and `update()` [3]. Put all schema and data changes for the plugin in the `update()` method, which Shopware runs automatically when the plugin is installed or updated [1][3]. Do not use `updateDestructive()` for plugin changes, since plugin install and update never execute it [1][3]. Alternatively, you can generate a complete migration including the SQL for your entities with `./bin/console dal:migration:create --bundle=SwagBasicExample --entities=your_entity,your_other_entity`, which requires your plugin to be activated [6].

questions.question: My plugin needs an extra PHP library from Packagist. How do I add it so it also works when the plugin is installed from a zip?
questions.answer:
Declare the library in the `require` section of your plugin's `composer.json`, the same way as any PHP project [1][2]. How it gets installed then depends on how the plugin is distributed [1]:

- **Composer-managed or static plugins (recommended):** The project's root Composer installation resolves and installs the dependency automatically, so no extra steps are needed [1].
- **Zip-installed plugins (e.g., Shopware Store):** The project does not resolve the dependency. You must either let Shopware run Composer during installation by overriding `executeComposerCommands()`, or bundle the packages with your plugin [1].

The excerpts do not show the exact code for overriding `executeComposerCommands()` or the steps for bundling packages, so check the full dependency guide for those details.

questions.question: How do I give my plugin its own log channel?
questions.answer:
First, make sure your plugin loads package configuration from the `/Resources/config/packages` folder by adding this to your plugin's main class (in `build()`):

```php
$confDir = \rtrim($this->getPath(), '/'). '/Resources/config';

$configLoader->load($confDir. '/{packages}/*.yaml', 'glob');
```

[1]

Then create a channel with a unique name that identifies your plugin in `[plugin root]/src/Resources/config/packages/monolog.yaml`:

```yaml
monolog:
  channels: ['my_plugin_channel']
```

[1]

Monolog automatically registers a logger service scoped to your channel, which you can inject using the service ID `monolog.logger.my_plugin_channel` [1]. Optionally, add a handler that directs your channel to a file:

```yaml
monolog:
  channels: ['my_plugin_channel']

  handlers:
    myPluginLogHandler:
        type: rotating_file
        path: "%kernel.logs_dir%/my_plugin_%kernel.environment%.log"
        level: error
        channels: [ "my_plugin_channel"]
```

[1]

This approach lets project owners redirect your channel to a different handler [1].

questions.question: How do I override Bootstrap SCSS variables such as $border-radius in my theme?
questions.answer:
Add an `overrides.scss` entry point in your theme's `theme.json` before `@Storefront` in the `style` section:

```javascript
// <plugin root>/src/Resources/theme.json
"style": [
  "app/storefront/src/scss/overrides.scss", <-- Variable overrides
  "@Storefront",
  "app/storefront/src/scss/base.scss"
]
```
[1][2]

In `<plugin root>/src/Resources/app/storefront/src/scss/overrides.scss`, set the variable, for example:

```css
$border-radius: 0;
```
[2]

After saving the file, run `bin/console theme:compile` and check the Storefront in the browser [1][2]. Only add variable overrides to this file, not CSS selectors and properties [1][2]. Bootstrap 4 uses the `!default` flag, so variable overrides have to be declared before the Bootstrap defaults are loaded [2].

questions.question: I changed SCSS in my theme but nothing changes in the browser. Which command do I need to run?
questions.answer:
After changing SCSS, you need to compile your theme by running the `bin/console theme:compile` command in the terminal. Then reload the Storefront in your browser to check the changes. [2]

If you are actively developing and want automatic updates in the browser, start the dev-server with `shopware-cli project storefront-watch`, which starts a NodeJS web server on port `9998`; open the Storefront on `localhost:9998` to get live reload. [1]

If the theme is still not applied after compiling, run `bin/console theme:change` and then `bin/console theme:compile`, and if there are still no changes, run `bin/console cache:clear`. [3]

questions.question: How does a backend integration get an access token for the Admin API?
questions.answer:
Create an integration in the Administration under **Settings → System → Integrations** and make sure the toggle is set to "Administrator" [1]. Copy the Access key ID (maps to `client_id`) and the Secret access key (maps to `client_secret`) [1]. Then request an OAuth token from your local Shopware instance:

```bash
curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/oauth/token" \
 -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
 "grant_type": "client_credentials",
 "client_id": "YOUR_ACCESS_KEY_ID",
 "client_secret": "YOUR_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY"
 }'
```

[1] The response contains an `access_token`, which you use as the Bearer token for authenticated Admin API requests [1]. The password grant with the `administration` client is only a local development shortcut and is not the recommended approach for integrations [3].

questions.question: How do I create my own Store API endpoint in a plugin?
questions.answer: Create a route class that extends the abstract route, with the Store API route scope attribute, a `getDecorated()` method that throws `DecorationPatternException`, and a `load` method returning a `StoreApiResponse`-based response. Example class file: `<plugin root>/src/Core/Content/Example/SalesChannel/ExampleRoute.php`, which defines `#[Route(path: '/store-api/example', name: 'store-api.example.search', methods: ['GET','POST'], defaults: ['_entity' => 'swag_example'])]` on `load()` [3]. Store API routes must be services and use named routes [4]. The route class, service definition and the `routes.php` import form one feature, and the generator normally creates them together [3]. Verify registration with `./bin/console debug:router store-api.example.search` [1]. Optionally, add an OpenAPI JSON file at `<plugin root>/src/Resources/Schema/StoreApi/example.json` so it appears in the Stoplight page [1]. The excerpts do not contain the exact service definition or `routes.php` contents, so those details are not covered.

questions.question: How can I change the response of an existing Store API route from my plugin?
questions.answer: To change the response of an existing Store API route, you override it by decorating the route. Create a new class that extends the abstract route class (e.g. `AbstractExampleRoute`), named for example `ExampleRouteDecorator`, and place it under `<plugin root>/src/Core/Content/Example/SalesChannel/ExampleRouteDecorator.php` [3]. The constructor must accept an instance of `AbstractExampleRoute`, and the `getDecorated()` method must return the decorated route passed into the constructor [3]. The decorator class carries the same route attribute with the Store API scope: `#[Route(defaults: [PlatformRequest::ATTRIBUTE_ROUTE_SCOPE => [StoreApiRouteScope::ID]])]` [3][2]. In the `load` method, call the decorated route first with `$this->decorated->load()`, then modify the returned response, for example by adding headers, and return it [3]. Store API response decorators must extend `StoreApiResponse` [2]. The excerpt's sample code calls `$this->decorated->load()` without arguments, while the signature takes `Criteria $criteria, SalesChannelContext $context`, so pass them through as needed; the excerpt does not explain this further.

questions.question: How can I make the API return only a few fields of an entity, and how is that different from includes?
questions.answer: Partial data loading lets you select specific fields of an entity to be returned by the API, which reduces response size and can improve performance [2]. Shopware's documentation does not show the exact request syntax for enabling it per request, so I cannot give a concrete request example from the excerpts [2]. The `includes` parameter is a search criteria option that restricts returned fields, for example `"includes": { "product": ["id", "name"] }` [3]. The key difference is where the filtering happens: `includes` works as post-output processing, so the complete entity is loaded on the backend and then filtered, while partial data loading works at the database level so only the requested fields are loaded [2]. Also, partial data loading only works at the entity level and cannot be used with custom responses such as the Store API product detail page or CMS; for a small response in those cases the documentation recommends `includes` [1].

questions.question: Which request header selects the language in which entities are returned by the API?
questions.answer:
The `sw-language-id` header selects the language. By default, the API returns entities in the system language, and this can be changed by specifying a language ID using the `sw-language-id` header [1].

```bash
POST /api/search/product
--header 'sw-language-id: be01bd336c204f20ab86eab45bbdbe45'
```
[1]

If a translation is missing for a field, the plain field will be `null`, so display-only clients should read from `translated` [1][2].

questions.question: How should the message queue be processed on a production server?
questions.answer: On a production system, the message queue should be processed via CLI processes instead of the Admin worker (browser in the Administration) [1][2]. This way, messages are completed regardless of logged-in Administration users and CPU load [1]. It is recommended to run one or more `messenger:consume` workers [2]. To automatically restart the processes after they stopped because of exceeding the given limits, you can use a process control system like systemd or supervisor [1][2]. Alternatively, a cron job can run the command periodically, but cron does not manage the maximum number of running workers like supervisor does [2]. It is also recommended to use a third-party message queue such as RabbitMQ to support multiple consumers and/or larger amounts of data to index [2][5]. Additionally, it is recommended to define your own message queue in addition to the standard one [1].

questions.question: How are scheduled tasks triggered on a production system?
questions.answer:
To run scheduled tasks, you must set up a background worker like the Message Queue and run the command `bin/console scheduled-task:run`. The command schedules all tasks to the queue and waits until a task needs to be scheduled. It consumes little CPU time or memory. [2] You can use the flag `--no-wait` and run the command from an operating system scheduler like cron. Check your scheduled task interval to determine the best interval to trigger the command. Example:

```bash
*/5 * * * * /usr/bin/php /var/www/html/bin/console scheduled-task:run --no-wait
``` [2] Alternatively, scheduled tasks can be run as part of your queue workers with the symfony scheduler component using `bin/console messenger:consume scheduler_shopware`, but this feature is experimental and available starting with Shopware 6.6. [4]

retrieved.heading: Using the symfony scheduler to run tasks

questions.question: How can I run one specific scheduled task right now for debugging, without the queue?
questions.answer:
You can run a single scheduled task directly, without the queue, using `bin/console scheduled-task:run-single <task-name>`. [1][2] Example:

```shell
bin/console scheduled-task:run-single log_entry.cleanup
```

[1][2] This command is available starting with Shopware 6.7.2.0. [1][2]

questions.question: Which environment variable turns Shopware's HTTP cache on or off?
questions.answer: The environment variable is `SHOPWARE_HTTP_CACHE_ENABLED`. It enables the HTTP cache, and its default value is `1` [1][3]. To enable it, set `SHOPWARE_HTTP_CACHE_ENABLED=1` in the `.env` file [6]. Basic HTTP cache configuration takes place in the `.env.local` file [3].

questions.question: What is the expected format of the DATABASE_URL environment variable?
questions.answer: The expected format is a DSN connection string: `mysql://user:password@host:port/dbname` [1]. It is a MySQL or MariaDB connection string [1]. For TLS connections, use the `DATABASE_SSL_*` environment variables instead of query parameters [1]. Example from the Deployment Helper docs: `mysql://user:pass@host:3306/shop` [2].

questions.question: How do I enable Elasticsearch/OpenSearch for the storefront search and build the index?
questions.answer:
1. Install the Elasticsearch integration if your project doesn't have it yet: `composer require shopware/elasticsearch` [2]. You need a supported OpenSearch (or Elasticsearch) server and running message queue workers [2].

2. Set the environment variables. For search and indexing, use:

```bash
OPENSEARCH_URL="elasticsearchhostname:9200"
SHOPWARE_ES_ENABLED="1"
SHOPWARE_ES_INDEXING_ENABLED="1"
```

This combination enables full support, with both search and indexing active [5]. The example file uses `SHOPWARE_ES_INDEX_PREFIX="sw"` and `SHOPWARE_ES_THROW_EXCEPTION=0` [5]. If a server should only read the index and not update it, set `SHOPWARE_ES_INDEXING_ENABLED=0` [5].

3. Build the search index after the services are running:

```bash
bin/console es:index
```

This command is shown in the Devenv setup, after OpenSearch is started [3]. The excerpts do not show it in a non-Devenv context.

Note: the search configuration of Shopware has no effect when using Elasticsearch. To configure which fields are searchable, you must install the Advanced Search extension [4].

The `es:admin:index` command and the `ADMIN_OPENSEARCH_URL` settings relate to the Administration, not the storefront, so they are not part of this setup [4].

questions.question: Can I set system configuration values in YAML files so they override what is stored in the database?
questions.answer:
Yes. Static system configuration lets you define system configuration values in `config/packages/<name>.yaml` under `shopware.system_config`, and these overwrite the values stored in the database [3][4]. Example:

```yaml
shopware:
  system_config:
    default:
      core.listing.allowBuyInListing: true
```

[3] The statically set configuration is an overlay of the database loaded configuration: if a key is set in both places, the value from `config/packages` is used, and the user can no longer change that configuration in the Administration [4][2]. This feature is available since Shopware 6.6.4.0 [4].
